A wrong (noun) is an act that is unjust, harmful, or unfair — something that should not have happened because it violates what is right. It is not simply a mistake or an accident. A mistake is something done without bad intent or through carelessness. A wrong is heavier than that: it involves a real violation of moral, ethical, or legal standards, and it almost always causes harm or injustice to someone.

Think of it this way: if you accidentally break someone's vase, that is a mistake. But if you cheat someone out of their money, betray someone's trust, or deny someone what they deserve — that is a wrong.
Two Ways "Wrong" Is Used as a Noun

1. As a countable noun — a specific unjust act

Here, "wrong" refers to a particular harmful or unjust act done to a person or group. You can say "a wrong" or "wrongs" (plural).

  • "He never forgot the wrong that had been done to him."
  • "The survivors demanded justice for the wrongs they had suffered."
  • "She spent years trying to right the wrong she had committed."

This use is deeply personal. A wrong is done to someone. The person who suffers it is a victim. The person who commits it is the offender. The wrong itself is the act that caused the injustice.

2. As an abstract noun — the concept of moral incorrectness

Here, "wrong" does not refer to any single act. It refers to the general idea of what is morally bad, unethical, or unjust — the entire category of immoral behaviour. This is almost always seen alongside its opposite, "right."

  • "Children must learn the difference between right and wrong."
  • "She has a strong sense of right and wrong."
  • "He knew it was wrong, and he did it anyway."

In this sense, "right" and "wrong" together form the two sides of morality — what ought to be done versus what ought not to be done. "Wrong" here is the whole domain of things that are unjust, harmful, or immoral.
The Central Quality of a Wrong: It Demands to Be Fixed

One of the most important things to understand about the noun "wrong" is that it carries a built-in sense that something needs to be corrected. Wrongs are not simply unfortunate events — they are injustices that call out for a response. This is why the most common verb paired with the noun "wrong" is "to right" (meaning: to correct or repair).

  • "She dedicated her life to righting wrongs."
  • "This verdict does nothing to right the wrong done to that family."
  • "He wanted to right the wrong before he died."

You can also "address," "remedy," or "redress" a wrong — all of these mean to correct or compensate for the injustice that was caused.

This quality is what separates "wrong" (noun) from "mistake." You fix a mistake. But you right a wrong — because a wrong is a matter of justice, not just correction.
Wrong in Moral and Legal Contexts

Moral wrong:
A moral wrong is an act that violates ethical principles — honesty, fairness, compassion, human dignity. Lying to hurt someone, betraying a friend, exploiting a vulnerable person, or treating someone as less than they are worth — these are all moral wrongs. They are judged not by courts, but by conscience and by society's shared values.

Legal wrong:
In law, a "wrong" means an act that violates a person's rights as defined by the law. Legal wrongs fall into two main types:

  • Criminal wrong: An act that breaks criminal law — such as theft, assault, or fraud. The state itself prosecutes the person who committed it.
  • Civil wrong (also called a "tort"): An act that causes harm to a specific person but may not be a crime in the criminal sense. Examples include negligence (a doctor who fails to provide proper care), defamation (saying false things that damage someone's reputation), or trespassing. The harmed person can take the offender to court and seek compensation.

This is why legal language is full of phrases like "the wrong done to the plaintiff," "the defendant committed a wrong," and "civil wrongs."

"Right a wrong"
To fix or correct an unjust act from the past.
"The new law was designed to right a historical wrong."

"Suffer a wrong"
To be the victim of an unjust act.
"She suffered many wrongs in silence for years."

"Do someone a wrong"
To treat someone unjustly or cause them harm they did not deserve.
"He felt the system had done him a grave wrong."

"The wrongs of the past"
Historical injustices done to people or groups that were never corrected.
"The movement seeks acknowledgment of the wrongs of the past."

"In the wrong"
To be the person at fault — the one who acted unjustly or incorrectly. ("Wrong" here is a noun used as the object of the preposition "in.")
"She was clearly in the wrong, and she knew it."

"Two wrongs don't make a right"
This famous saying means: doing something bad in response to someone else's bad act does not make the situation better, and it does not justify your action.
"I know he betrayed you, but spreading lies about him isn't okay — two wrongs don't make a right."

Wrong vs. Mistake
A mistake is an error — something unintentional, often due to ignorance or carelessness. A wrong involves a violation of what is right, usually with real harm caused to someone. You forgive mistakes; you seek justice for wrongs.

Wrong vs. Sin
A sin is a wrong that is defined in a religious or spiritual framework — a violation of divine law or religious principles. A wrong is a broader, secular concept that applies in moral, ethical, and legal contexts too — regardless of religion.

Wrong vs. Injustice
Injustice is closely related but tends to be broader and more systemic — the state of a society, institution, or system that is unfair. A wrong is usually specific and personal — a particular act done to a particular person or group. All wrongs are unjust, but injustice can describe a whole system, while a wrong describes an act within it.

Wrong vs. Harm
Harm is damage or injury caused to someone. A wrong is harm that is unjust — that should not have happened and that someone is responsible for. Not all harms are wrongs (a natural disaster causes harm but no "wrong"), but all wrongs involve harm of some kind.

"Wrong" (noun) is a weighty word. It carries moral gravity and emotional seriousness. When someone calls an act "a wrong," they are not being casual — they are making a moral judgment, saying that something was fundamentally unjust and that it mattered.

You would not use "wrong" (noun) for trivial things. You would not say "arriving five minutes late was a wrong" — that would sound unnatural and overdramatic. The noun "wrong" is reserved for acts that genuinely violate fairness, dignity, rights, or morality. For small everyday errors, you would say "mistake," "fault," or "error."

It is a word that appears often in serious, formal, or emotionally charged contexts: speeches about justice, court proceedings, philosophical writing, literature, and sincere personal accounts of being treated unfairly.

As a noun, "wrong" means:

  • A specific unjust, harmful, or unfair act done to someone — a violation of what is right ("a wrong," "wrongs")
  • The abstract moral concept of what is bad, unethical, or unjust, as opposed to what is right ("right and wrong")

It always implies that something ought to have been different. It is personal — wrongs are done to people. It demands correction — wrongs beg to be righted. And it carries real moral weight — you use this word when you mean to say that something genuinely violated the standards of what is fair, decent, and just.
